metadata.title: The use of digital devices for schoolwork at home and reading achievement: Multilevel analyses of the PIRLS 2016 U.S. results

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PIRLS 2016 fourth-grade U.S. student data and estimates multilevel models in Mplus (Version 8.9). The authors report that all estimates except for the frequency/descriptive statistics were weighted to ensure national representation for fourth-grade students in the United States, using the student weight variable TOTWGT throughout the models. Missing data were handled via full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in Mplus, which uses all available information under MAR/MCAR assumptions rather than listwise deletion. The manuscript does not mention replicate-weight methods (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so uncertainty is presented based on the model-based standard errors under the specified multilevel specification.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values handling is not applicable because the dependent variable is treated as a PIRLS reading achievement score used directly in multilevel regression (not as an explicitly PV-based outcome with PV replication/combining rules described in the text). Missing-data handling is implemented via full information maximum likelihood (FIML) in Mplus, which is not a standard PV-combining workflow; the paper does not describe PV-specific missingness handling. This means the analysis relies on the authors’ FIML approach for missing questionnaire/covariate data rather than reporting a PV-specific procedure.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Analytic sample consists of PIRLS 2016 fourth-grade students in the United States (N=4425). The authors state that the complete Ns for students are 4425, but most variables have missing data; missing imputations were done for the main analysis using FIML in Mplus. The models are multilevel with students nested in schools; the study also stratifies students into reading performance groups based on PIRLS 2016 reading benchmarks (initially five groups, then Groups 1 and 2 merged due to sample size limitations/empty cells).

main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression coefficients (B, SE) reported; no ML metrics (e.g., Accuracy/AUC/R²) reported. Model 2: weekly use B = −8.62 (SE = 3.19, p < .01); daily use B = −24.74 (SE = 2.77, p < .001). Model 3 (with interactions): weekly use B = −16.74 (SE = 4.52, p < .001); daily use B = −33.12 (SE = 3.82, p < .001). Gender interaction terms: weekly interaction B = 17.10 (SE = 6.39, p < .01); daily interaction B = 17.68 (SE = 5.76, p < .01). Additional analysis (Reading achievement by reading performance group (low/intermediate/high/advanced)): Stratified multilevel models (Table 3). Low-performing (merged Groups 1–2): no significant associations for tablet/computer use frequency. Intermediate-performing (Group 3): no significant associations. High-performing (Group 4): daily use B = −3.73 (SE = 1.28, p < .01). Advanced-performing (Group 5): monthly use B = 5.46 (SE = 2.69, p < .05). No significant gender interactions within any reading performance group.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 Reading (United States) the study leveraged test language use at home, home tablet/computer possession, school SES, school location, and shortage of school resources to model reading achievement, finding that tablet/computer use for schoolwork at home was inversely associated with reading achievement for weekly and daily users (e.g., B = −8.62 for weekly and B = −24.74 for daily in Model 2). This indicates that frequent at-home device use for schoolwork may be linked to lower reading outcomes for many students, suggesting that guidance on focused, regulated use at home may be necessary rather than assuming that more frequent device use automatically improves literacy.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes PIRLS 2016 Grade 4 reading achievement for the United States (N=4,425) to examine how tablet/computer use for schoolwork at home relates to reading performance. Using multilevel models in Mplus, the authors apply the student weight TOTWGT for national representativeness and handle missing covariate data with full information maximum likelihood (FIML). In the overall models, weekly and daily at-home device use is associated with lower reading achievement compared with non-use (Model 2: B = −8.62 for weekly and B = −24.74 for daily). Gender interactions show that these negative associations are more pronounced for male students than female students. Subgroup analyses by PIRLS 2016 reading benchmarks indicate heterogeneity: high-performing students show a negative association for daily use (B = −3.73), while advanced-performing students show a positive association for monthly use (B = 5.46). The authors caution that cross-sectional associations should not be interpreted causally.
